narration.text: About two billion years ago, Earth had nuclear reactors. Nobody built them. In 1972, uranium from Gabon held less uranium-235 than expected. Fission fingerprints in the rock revealed ancient nuclear reactions. How could geology sustain them? Back then, uranium had a higher share of that easily split isotope. Geology concentrated it into rich deposits. Splitting uranium released neutrons. Collisions with hydrogen in groundwater slowed them, helping them split more uranium. Enough avoided escape or absorption elsewhere to keep the chain going. From one studied zone's isotopes, researchers infer starts and stops: heating drove water away; cooling let it return. Reaction zones in rock. Heat, not electricity. Earth had assembled the conditions for fission, without machinery.

factualSafeguards: Natural fission zones in rock, not human-built machinery or electricity generation.
Approximate two-billion-year age, not a precise common start date for every zone.
Ancient fissile fraction, concentration/geometry, neutron retention, competing absorption and moderation are jointly relevant.
Water slows neutrons through collisions, especially hydrogen; moderation is distinct from absorption.
Present depleted uranium and fission products provide evidence of ancient fission; operational details are reconstructed.
Cycling explicitly scoped to one studied reaction zone; groundwater feedback is an inference, no universal precise pulse clock.
Original illustrative geological and atomic views, not site footage, exact ancient geometry, quantitative neutron paths or visible radioactivity.
unusualProduction: Discovery-led Earth, laboratory sample and qualitative evidence; deep-time reconstruction, connected neutron/water mechanism and qualified feedback; voice and silence.
